p5-1.a: Microsoft's open-source ORM for .NET: it maps classes to tables, translates LINQ to SQL, tracks changes and manages migrations, with providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite and more.
p5-1.qa: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM for .NET: it maps classes to tables, translates LINQ to SQL, tracks changes to entities and writes them back in SaveChanges, and manages schema through migrations. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Cosmos DB and more through providers.
i: Core pieces: DbContext (unit of work), DbSet (tables), change tracker, model built from conventions, attributes and Fluent API.
EF Core 8: complex types, raw SQL for unmapped types, JSON columns; EF Core 9/10: better LINQ translation, named query filters (10), LeftJoin operator (10), vector search for SQL Server.
Performance tools: AsNoTracking, compiled models, compiled queries, ExecuteUpdate/Delete, DbContext pooling.
In IRT: EF Core for most CRUD and domain writes, Dapper or raw SQL for heavy reporting.
f: Is EF Core slow?
Not inherently; most problems come from query shape (N+1, over-fetching, tracking).
What's new in EF Core 10?
LeftJoin/RightJoin LINQ operators, named query filters, JSON and vector improvements.

p5-2.a: ADO.NET: raw connections, commands and readers; fastest and most control, but manual SQL and mapping.|EF Core: LINQ, change tracking, migrations and productivity, with a small overhead.|Use EF Core for most CRUD, and Dapper or ADO.NET for hot paths and complex reporting SQL.
p5-2.qa: ADO.NET gives raw connections, commands and data readers: fastest and full control, but manual SQL and mapping. EF Core adds LINQ, change tracking, migrations and relationships for productivity, with some overhead. Dapper sits between: you write SQL, it maps results fast.
i: EF Core itself uses ADO.NET underneath.
Choose EF Core for domain writes and typical queries; Dapper/raw SQL for complex reports or bulk paths.
SqlBulkCopy for very large inserts.
Both must use parameters to avoid SQL injection.
f: Can you mix EF Core and Dapper?
Yes, even sharing the same connection and transaction.
When is raw ADO.NET justified?
Extreme performance paths, streaming large results, or special features like table-valued parameters.

p5-3.a: DbContext: a session with the database, combining unit of work, change tracker and connection management; the model is configured in OnModelCreating.|DbSet<T>: a queryable collection that represents a table, used to query, add and remove entities.
p5-3.qa: DbContext is a session with the database combining unit of work, change tracker and connection management; the model is configured in OnModelCreating. DbSet<T> represents a table you query with LINQ and add or remove entities from.
i: DbContext is not thread-safe and is registered as scoped; one per request or unit of work.
AddDbContextPool reuses instances for performance; IDbContextFactory for background or Blazor.
Configurations split into IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> classes and ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly.
f: What happens if two threads use one DbContext?
EF throws "A second operation was started on this context"; use separate contexts.
Context pooling caveat?
State must be reset; don't store per-request data in context fields.

p5-4.a: Include loads a navigation of the root entity; ThenInclude loads the next level from that navigation, for example `Studies.Include(s => s.Sites).ThenInclude(x => x.Shipments)`.|Deep includes can explode rows; consider AsSplitQuery or projections.
p5-4.qa: Include loads a navigation of the root entity; ThenInclude loads the next level from that navigation, e.g. Studies.Include(s => s.Sites).ThenInclude(site => site.Shipments). Filtered includes (EF Core 5+) restrict loaded children with Where, OrderBy and Take.
i: Multiple collection includes can cause a cartesian explosion; AsSplitQuery runs separate queries.
Projection with Select is often better than Include for read-only views.
Include is ignored if you project to a non-entity type.
f: What is a cartesian explosion?
Joining several collections multiplies rows, sending huge duplicate data.
Split query downside?
Multiple round-trips and possible inconsistency without a transaction.

p5-5.a: `dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentIndex` generates Up and Down code from model changes; review it like any code, then produce an idempotent script with `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent` for the release.
p5-5.qa: dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentIndex generates Up and Down code from model changes, which I review like any code; then I generate an idempotent SQL script (dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent) or a migration bundle for the pipeline, so DBAs and the regulated release process can review and run it.
i: Don't call Database.Migrate() at app startup in production with multiple instances (race conditions); run migrations as a pipeline step.
Migration bundles (efbundle) are self-contained executables.
Data migrations and expand/contract for zero-downtime.
Model snapshot file must be committed and merged carefully.
f: Why idempotent scripts?
They can run against any environment state safely, checking applied migrations.
How do you resolve migration conflicts between branches?
Remove and re-create the later migration after merging, or merge snapshots carefully.

p5-6.a: Code First: the C# model is the source of truth and migrations create the schema.|Database First: scaffold entities from an existing database (`dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold`), good for legacy schemas owned by DBAs.
p5-6.qa: In Code First the C# model is the source of truth and migrations create and evolve the schema; in Database First you scaffold entities from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold) and the database stays the source of truth. IRT uses [Code First for newer services and scaffolding for legacy schemas].
i: Code First suits greenfield services owning their data.
Database First suits shared or DBA-owned databases.
EF Core Power Tools helps with reverse engineering.
Hybrid: scaffold once from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold), then continue Code First with migrations.
f: Can you switch later?
Yes, by creating a baseline migration from the existing schema.
How do you keep scaffolded code customisable?
Partial classes and templates (T4) so re-scaffolding doesn't overwrite custom code.

p5-7.a: LINQ queries over DbSet/IQueryable that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; only translatable methods are allowed in the query.
p5-7.qa: LINQ-to-Entities is LINQ over DbSet/IQueryable that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; only translatable methods are allowed in filters (Where, Select, OrderBy, string Contains/StartsWith, EF.Functions). The query is an expression tree until enumerated.
i: ToQueryString() shows the SQL without running it.
EF.Functions.Like, DateDiffDay and others map to SQL functions.
Final Select projections can call client code (top-level only).
The provider translates expression trees to SQL; ToQueryString() shows the SQL without executing it.
f: What triggers execution?
Enumeration: ToList, First, Count, foreach, await ToListAsync.
How do you see generated SQL quickly?
query.ToQueryString() or logging.

p5-8.a: Using methods EF cannot translate (custom C# functions, some string operations) inside a filter. EF Core 3+ throws instead of silently loading every row, except in the final Select projection.|Calling AsEnumerable or ToList too early also pulls data into memory before filtering.
p5-8.qa: Client-side evaluation happens when you use methods EF can't translate (custom C# functions, some string or date operations) inside a filter. Since EF Core 3, it throws instead of silently loading everything into memory; only the final projection may run client code.
i: Fixes: rewrite with translatable methods, EF.Functions, computed columns, or map a database function with HasDbFunction.
AsEnumerable() explicitly switches to in-memory after filtering in SQL.
Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions in Where throw instead of silently evaluating on the client; only the final Select projection may run client-side.
Common causes: calling your own C# methods in Where, string.Format, or unsupported overloads; fix with translatable expressions or a mapped DB function.
f: Why did EF Core 3 change this?
Silent client evaluation loaded whole tables and caused serious performance issues.
Is AsEnumerable dangerous?
Only if used before filtering, which loads too much data.

p5-9.a: AsNoTracking for reads; project to DTOs with Select; filter and page in SQL; avoid N+1 with Include or projections; AsSplitQuery for large includes.|Proper indexes, compiled queries for hot paths, ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete for bulk changes, DbContext pooling.|Log the generated SQL and check execution plans.

steps.title: AsNoTracking
steps.detail: Read-only queries skip the change tracker

steps.title: Project with Select
steps.detail: Only the columns the DTO needs

steps.title: Measure
steps.detail: Log SQL, read the plan, add indexes

p5-9.qa: I use AsNoTracking for reads, project to DTOs with Select, filter and page in SQL, avoid N+1 with Include or projections, use AsSplitQuery for multiple collections, add the right indexes, batch writes, use ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete for set-based changes, and measure with logged SQL and execution plans.
i: DbContext pooling and compiled models reduce startup and per-request overhead.
Avoid lazy loading in APIs.
Check for implicit conversions and non-SARGable predicates in generated SQL.
The shipment-list fix: index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE plus projection took [9 s to under 300 ms].
f: How do you detect N+1?
Log SQL and look for repeated similar queries per row, or use MiniProfiler.
AsNoTracking vs AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution?
The latter de-duplicates entity instances without tracking.

p5-10.a: SaveChanges detects changes and writes every pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in one transaction.|SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking the thread during I/O; use it in ASP.NET Core.
p5-10.qa: SaveChanges detects changes in tracked entities and writes all pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements in one transaction, batching them where possible. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking a thread during I/O, which is what I use in ASP.NET Core.
i: Returns the number of affected rows; throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException or DbUpdateException.
Interceptors (SaveChangesInterceptor) for auditing and soft delete.
ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled can be turned off for bulk adds.
SaveChanges wraps all changes in one transaction by default and batches statements (SQL Server batching).
f: Is SaveChanges transactional?
Yes, each call is one transaction unless you've started an explicit one.
Why call SaveChanges once per unit of work?
Fewer round-trips and all-or-nothing behaviour.

p5-11.a: EF Core 7+ ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete run set-based SQL without loading rows; AddRange with batching for inserts.|For very large loads use SqlBulkCopy or a bulk-extensions library, in chunks inside transactions.
p5-11.qa: EF Core 7+ ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete run set-based SQL without loading entities; AddRange with batching handles moderate inserts. For very large loads I use SqlBulkCopy (or a library like EFCore.BulkExtensions) into a staging table, then MERGE set-based.
i: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker and interceptors; handle auditing separately.
Batch size (MaxBatchSize) affects round-trips.
Wrap staging plus merge in a transaction.
c:
await db.Shipments.Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.Pending && s.CreatedAt < cutoff)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(u => u.SetProperty(s => s.Status, ShipmentStatus.Expired), ct);
f: Downside of ExecuteUpdate?
Tracked entities in memory aren't updated, and SaveChanges interceptors don't run.
How fast is SqlBulkCopy?
Hundreds of thousands of rows per second, depending on table and indexes.

p5-12.a: EF.CompileAsyncQuery caches the LINQ-to-SQL translation of a query shape, saving translation cost on very hot paths.|EF already caches most query plans, so use it only after measuring.
p5-12.qa: EF.CompileAsyncQuery caches the LINQ-to-SQL translation of a query shape so very hot paths skip translation cost. EF already caches translations internally, so compiled queries give only small gains; compiled models (dotnet ef dbcontext optimize) help startup for large models.
i: EF Core 9+ supports precompiled queries for native AOT (experimental).
Use only after profiling shows translation cost matters.
EF Core already caches query plans; compiled queries mainly save the expression-tree compare and translation cost on very hot paths.
c:
static readonly Func<IrtDbContext, int, Task<Shipment?>> ById =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((IrtDbContext db, int id) => db.Shipments.FirstOrDefault(s => s.Id == id));
f: When are compiled queries worth it?
Extremely hot, simple queries in high-throughput services.
What is a compiled model?
A generated model that avoids building the model at startup.

p5-13.a: `LogTo(Console.WriteLine)` on the options builder, or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command log category at Information; `ToQueryString()` on a query; EnableSensitiveDataLogging only in development.
p5-13.qa: Use LogTo(Console.WriteLine) on the options builder, or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command log category at Information, which logs SQL and timing. EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows parameter values, for development only.
i: ToQueryString() for one query.
Interceptors (DbCommandInterceptor) can log slow queries or add query tags.
TagWith("ShipmentList") adds comments to SQL to find it in Query Store.
In tests or dev: optionsBuilder.LogTo(Console.WriteLine, LogLevel.Information); never EnableSensitiveDataLogging in production.
f: Why not enable sensitive data logging in production?
It logs parameter values that may contain personal data.
How do you find which code issued a slow query?
TagWith or TagWithCallSite to add identifying comments.

p5-14.a: Configure with navigations and foreign keys by convention or Fluent API (HasOne/WithMany, HasMany/WithMany).|One-to-one: Subject and ConsentRecord. One-to-many: Site and Shipments. Many-to-many: Users and Studies, with an explicit join entity when the link has data (role, assigned date).
p5-14.qa: Relationships are configured with navigations and foreign keys by convention or Fluent API (HasOne/WithMany, HasMany/WithMany). One-to-one: Subject and Consent; one-to-many: Study and Sites; many-to-many: Users and Studies, with EF Core 5+ creating the join table automatically or using an explicit join entity with extra data.
i: Delete behaviour: Cascade, Restrict, SetNull, configured per relationship.
Required vs optional by FK nullability.
Explicit join entities when the join has data (role, assigned date).
c:
b.Entity<Site>().HasOne(s => s.Study).WithMany(st => st.Sites).HasForeignKey(s => s.StudyId).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
b.Entity<User>().HasMany(u => u.Studies).WithMany(s => s.Users).UsingEntity<StudyAssignment>();
f: Why Restrict on delete?
To avoid accidental cascades deleting regulated data.
What are multiple cascade paths?
SQL Server rejects schemas where deletes can cascade by more than one path.

p5-15.a: Properties that exist in the EF model and table but not in the C# class, such as LastModifiedBy or a foreign key, accessed with `EF.Property<T>(entity, name)`; handy for audit columns.
p5-15.qa: Shadow properties exist in the EF model and table but not in the C# class, such as LastModifiedBy or a foreign key; they're accessed with EF.Property<T>(entity, "Name") in queries and through the change tracker. They keep infrastructure concerns like audit columns out of domain classes.
i: Set them in a SaveChanges interceptor.
Query filters can use them (soft delete IsDeleted).
Common use: audit columns (CreatedAt, UpdatedBy) set in SaveChanges via ChangeTracker without polluting the domain model.
f: When would EF create a shadow FK?
When a navigation exists without an FK property in the class.
Downside?
Less discoverable in code.

p5-16.a: Value objects mapped as part of their owner with OwnsOne/OwnsMany, for example an Address inside Site stored in the Site table's columns; they have no identity of their own.
p5-16.qa: Owned entities map value objects as part of their owner with OwnsOne/OwnsMany, e.g. an Address inside Site stored in the Site table's columns; they have no identity of their own. EF Core 8 complex types (ComplexProperty) are a newer option for value objects with value semantics, and owned types can be mapped to JSON columns.
i: Value objects: immutable, compared by value (Money, Address, TemperatureRange).
OwnsMany can map to a separate table or JSON.
Owned types can map to the same table (columns prefixed) or a separate table; in EF Core 8, complex types are an alternative for value objects.
c:
b.Entity<Site>().OwnsOne(s => s.Address);   // Address_City, Address_Country columns
b.Entity<Site>().ComplexProperty(s => s.StorageRange);  // EF Core 8 complex type
f: Owned type vs complex type?
Owned types are entity types with hidden keys; complex types are true value types without identity.
Why JSON columns?
Flexible nested data queried with JSON functions without extra tables.

p5-17.a: Fluent API `HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status })` with IsUnique, HasFilter or IncludeProperties (SQL Server), or the [Index] attribute; created through migrations.
p5-17.qa: Fluent API HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status }) with IsUnique, HasFilter or IncludeProperties (SQL Server), or the [Index] attribute on the class; migrations then create the index. I base indexes on real query patterns and verify with execution plans.
i: Unique indexes enforce business rules (one kit number per study).
Filtered indexes for hot subsets.
Name indexes explicitly for stable migrations.
c:
b.Entity<Shipment>().HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status, s.ShipmentDate })
 .IncludeProperties(s => new { s.SiteId, s.KitCount }).HasDatabaseName("IX_Shipments_Study_Status_Date");
f: What does IncludeProperties do?
Adds INCLUDE columns so the index covers the query.
Unique index vs unique constraint?
Functionally similar in SQL Server; a constraint expresses intent and is backed by an index.

p5-18.a: Primary key: uniquely identifies each row, not null, one per table (clustered by default in SQL Server).|Foreign key: a column referencing another table's primary key, enforcing referential integrity, with cascade rules.
p5-18.qa: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, can't be null, and there's one per table (clustered by default in SQL Server). A foreign key is a column referencing another table's primary or unique key, enforcing referential integrity so you can't have orphan rows.
i: Surrogate keys (identity, sequence, GUID) vs natural keys (kit number).
GUID PKs: use sequential GUIDs (NEWSEQUENTIALID, or Guid.CreateVersion7 in .NET 9) to avoid fragmentation.
Index foreign key columns; SQL Server doesn't do it automatically.
Choose surrogate keys (int/bigint identity or sequential GUID) for stability; natural keys can change.
f: Should every FK be indexed?
Usually, for joins and to avoid locking scans on deletes of the parent.
What is Guid.CreateVersion7?
A .NET 9 API creating time-ordered UUIDv7 values, better for index locality.

p5-19.a: A unique constraint forbids duplicate values and is backed by a unique index.|One primary key vs many unique keys; the PK is not null, while a unique key allows one NULL in SQL Server; the PK is the identity, unique keys are alternate keys such as KitNumber.
p5-19.qa: A unique constraint forbids duplicate values and is backed by a unique index. A table has one primary key but can have many unique keys; the PK can't be null, while a unique key in SQL Server allows one NULL (use a filtered unique index to allow many).
i: Unique constraints enforce business rules regardless of app bugs or races.
Composite unique keys (StudyId, KitNumber).
A unique constraint allows one NULL in SQL Server; use a filtered unique index (WHERE col IS NOT NULL) to allow many NULLs.
c: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Users_Email ON dbo.Users(Email) WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;
f: Why enforce uniqueness in the database too?
Concurrent requests can both pass an app check.
Can a FK reference a unique key?
Yes, not only primary keys.

p5-20.a: An index on several columns, such as (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate). Column order matters: it supports seeks on the leading columns (leftmost prefix). Put equality columns first, then range columns.
p5-20.qa: A composite index covers several columns, such as (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate). Column order matters: it supports seeks on the leading column(s), so put equality-filtered columns first and range or sort columns after. It can serve queries on StudyId alone or StudyId plus Status, but not Status alone.
i: Leftmost prefix rule.
INCLUDE columns make it covering without widening the key.
Our shipment fix used exactly (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE, cutting reads from [400,000 to 2,000].
Our shipment index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE (...) served the main list query: equality columns first, the range/sort column last.
f: Why equality before range?
After a range column, later key columns can't be used for seeking.
Can SQL Server use a skip scan?
Not generally; it would scan instead.

p5-21.a: A non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (for example only Pending shipments): smaller and faster for queries on a hot subset. The query predicate must match the filter.
p5-21.qa: A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (e.g. only Pending shipments): smaller, cheaper to maintain and faster for queries on a hot subset. The query predicate must match the filter, and parameterised queries may not use it unless the optimizer can prove the match.
i: Great for status columns where few rows are "active".
Filtered unique indexes allow uniqueness only among non-null or active rows.
Requires specific SET options (QUOTED_IDENTIFIER, ANSI_NULLS).
Parameterized queries may not use a filtered index if the plan can't prove the filter matches; use literals or OPTION(RECOMPILE) when needed.
f: Why might a parameterised query ignore it?
The plan must be valid for any parameter value, so it can't rely on the filter.
Fix?
Use a literal for the filtered value or OPTION (RECOMPILE).

p5-22.a: Help: the B-tree lets SQL Server seek rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning, cover queries and avoid sorts.|Hurt: every insert, update and delete maintains them; they use storage and memory and cause page splits; unused or low-selectivity indexes are pure cost.
p5-22.qa: Indexes help because the B-tree lets SQL Server seek rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning, cover queries without lookups, and avoid sorts. They hurt when there are too many: every insert, update and delete must maintain them, they use storage and memory, and unused or duplicate indexes add cost without benefit.
i: Check sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats for unused indexes.
Key lookups on many rows can make a seek slower than a scan.
Fragmentation matters less on SSDs; statistics freshness matters more.
Monitor with sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats: indexes with many updates and no seeks are candidates to drop.
f: How many indexes are too many?
There's no fixed number; judge by write workload and usage stats.
What is a key lookup?
Fetching extra columns from the clustered index for each row found in a non-clustered index.

p5-23.a: The optimizer's recipe for a query: operators (seeks, scans, join types, sorts), estimated vs actual rows and costs.|Read the actual plan (SSMS, Query Store) to find scans, key lookups, spills and bad estimates.
p5-23.qa: An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for a query: operators (seeks, scans, join types, sorts), estimated vs actual row counts and costs. I read the actual plan to find scans, key lookups, bad estimates, spills and implicit conversions, and use Query Store to see plan history and regressions.
i: Read right to left, top to bottom; thick arrows mean many rows.
Warnings: implicit conversion, missing index, tempdb spills.
Join types: nested loops (small inputs), hash (large unsorted), merge (sorted inputs).
Query Store can force a known good plan.
f: Estimated vs actual plan?
Estimated shows the plan without running; actual adds real row counts.
What does a big estimate vs actual gap mean?
Stale statistics or parameter sniffing; investigate cardinality.

p5-24.a: Table scan: reads every row of a heap.|Index scan: reads all or a large range of an index.|Index seek: navigates the B-tree straight to the matching rows; best for selective predicates.
p5-24.qa: A table scan reads every row of a heap; an index scan reads all or a large range of an index (clustered index scan reads the whole table); an index seek navigates the B-tree directly to matching rows. Seeks are best for selective queries; scans can be fine for large portions of data.
i: Non-SARGable predicates (functions on columns, leading wildcards, implicit conversions) force scans.
Range scans are seeks with a range predicate.
Key lookups after a nonclustered seek can dominate cost; covering indexes with INCLUDE remove them.
c:
-- Non-SARGable: WHERE YEAR(ShipmentDate) = 2025
-- SARGable:    WHERE ShipmentDate >= '2025-01-01' AND ShipmentDate < '2026-01-01'
f: Is a scan always bad?
No, reading most of a small table is cheaper by scan.
What is SARGable?
A predicate that can use an index seek (Search ARGument able).

p5-25.a: Cardinality estimate: how many rows the optimizer expects at each step of the plan.|Statistics: histograms of column value distribution used for those estimates. Stale statistics cause bad estimates and bad plans (our plan-regression incident).
p5-25.qa: A cardinality estimate is how many rows the optimizer expects at each plan step; statistics are histograms of column value distributions (up to 200 steps) used to make those estimates. Bad estimates from stale or missing statistics lead to bad plans, like nested loops over millions of rows.
i: Auto update statistics triggers after a threshold of changes (dynamic threshold since SQL Server 2016).
UPDATE STATISTICS ... WITH FULLSCAN for skewed data.
Table variables historically estimated 1 row (improved with deferred compilation in SQL 2019).
Auto-update statistics triggers after a percentage of changes; large tables may need manual UPDATE STATISTICS after bulk loads.
f: Why did a plan change overnight in your incident?
A statistics update caused recompilation with an unrepresentative parameter value.
What is the cardinality estimator version?
The model tied to compatibility level; changes can shift plans after upgrades.

p5-26.a: UNION removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you need distinct rows.
p5-26.qa: UNION removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you truly need de-duplication.
i: Column count and types must match; names come from the first query.
ORDER BY applies to the whole result, at the end.
UNION adds a sort or hash distinct, which costs CPU and memory on large sets.
Use UNION ALL by default when sets can't overlap or duplicates are fine.
f: When is UNION needed?
When overlapping sources may return the same row and duplicates are wrong.
UNION vs JOIN?
UNION stacks rows vertically; JOIN combines columns horizontally.

p5-27.a: EXISTS stops at the first match; IN compares against a list or subquery. Modern optimizers often produce the same plan.|NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery contains a NULL, so prefer NOT EXISTS.
p5-27.qa: EXISTS stops at the first match; IN compares against a list or subquery. Modern optimizers often produce the same semi-join plan for both, but NOT IN with NULLs in the subquery returns no rows, so I prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins.
i: Large IN lists from apps create plan cache bloat; use table-valued parameters or JSON (OPENJSON).
EF Core 8+ translates Contains on lists using OPENJSON parameters.
NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns no rows; NOT EXISTS behaves as expected, so prefer it.
c: SELECT s.* FROM Sites s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id);
f: Why does NOT IN fail with NULL?
Comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole predicate isn't true.
How did EF Core 8 change Contains?
It sends the list as a JSON parameter, keeping one cached plan.

p5-28.a: CTE: a named query for one statement; not materialised; readable; supports recursion.|Temp table (#t): materialised in tempdb, can be indexed and reused across statements, and has statistics; better for large intermediate results.
p5-28.qa: A CTE is a named query for one statement: not materialised, readable, and supports recursion. A temp table (#t) is materialised in tempdb, can be indexed, has statistics and can be reused across statements in the session. Use CTEs for readability, temp tables for large intermediate results reused or needing indexes.
i: Table variables (@t) have limited statistics; good for small sets.
CTE referenced twice is evaluated twice.
Recursive CTEs for hierarchies (MAXRECURSION default 100).
Table variables have limited statistics (improved by deferred compilation in SQL Server 2019+); temp tables have full stats.
f: Is a CTE faster than a subquery?
No, it's the same; it's about readability.
Temp table vs table variable?
Temp tables have statistics and are better for larger data.

p5-29.a: ROW_NUMBER: unique sequence even for ties.|RANK: ties share a rank and leave gaps.|DENSE_RANK: ties share a rank with no gaps.
p5-29.qa: ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence even for ties; RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). All need OVER (ORDER BY ...), optionally PARTITION BY.
i: Deterministic ROW_NUMBER needs a unique ORDER BY (add a tie-breaker).
NTILE splits into buckets; LAG/LEAD access neighbouring rows.
Use ROW_NUMBER for pagination and dedup; DENSE_RANK for "nth highest" when ties count once.
c:
SELECT SiteId, KitCount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rn,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) drnk
FROM SiteStock;
f: Which for nth-highest distinct value?
DENSE_RANK.
Can you filter on a window function in WHERE?
No, wrap it in a CTE or subquery first.

p5-30.a: `SELECT KitNumber, COUNT(*) FROM Kits GROUP BY KitNumber HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;`|Or `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id)` and keep row 1, which also lets you delete the extras.
p5-30.qa: Group and count: SELECT KitNumber, COUNT(*) FROM Kits GROUP BY KitNumber HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. To see or delete the duplicate rows themselves, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id) and keep rn = 1.
i: Delete duplicates via a CTE where rn > 1, then add a unique constraint to prevent recurrence.
Delete duplicates keeping one: WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Users) DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1.
Prevent recurrence with a unique index after cleanup.
c:
WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudyId, KitNumber ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Kits)
DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;
f: Why can you delete from a CTE?
SQL Server allows DML through a CTE over a single base table.
What prevents new duplicates?
A unique constraint or index.

p5-31.a: `SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET N-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY;`|Or `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) = N`, which handles ties.|Second highest: `SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Emp WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Emp)`.
p5-31.qa: SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET N-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY; or DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) in a CTE and filter on rank = N, which handles ties correctly.
i: The classic MAX with subquery works for second highest only.
Return NULL when there's no nth value if required.
OFFSET/FETCH alternative: SELECT DISTINCT Salary ... ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY.
c:
WITH r AS (SELECT Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) dr FROM Emp)
SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM r WHERE dr = @N;
f: Why DENSE_RANK not ROW_NUMBER?
Ties would otherwise count as separate positions.
Per department?
Add PARTITION BY DepartmentId.

p5-32.a: `WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) AS rn FROM Shipments) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn <= 3;`|Or CROSS APPLY with TOP N per group.
p5-32.qa: Use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY: WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) rn FROM Shipments) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn <= 3. CROSS APPLY with TOP is an alternative that can be faster with a good index.
i: Index (SiteId, ShipDate DESC) supports both.
CROSS APPLY with TOP (N) ... ORDER BY can be faster than ROW_NUMBER when an index supports the per-group ordering.
Ties: use RANK or WITH TIES if equal values should all appear.
c:
SELECT s.Id, x.* FROM Sites s
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP (3) Id, ShipDate FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) x;
f: When is CROSS APPLY better?
When there are few groups and an index allows a seek per group.
Ties?
Use RANK or DENSE_RANK if ties should all be included.

p5-33.a: Dirty read: reading uncommitted data that may be rolled back.|Non-repeatable read: the same row returns different values within one transaction because another transaction updated it.|Phantom read: re-running a range query returns new rows inserted by another transaction.
p5-33.qa: A dirty read reads uncommitted data that may be rolled back; a non-repeatable read gets different values for the same row within a transaction because another transaction updated it; a phantom read finds new rows on re-running a range query because another transaction inserted them.
i: Read Uncommitted (NOLOCK) allows dirty reads; Read Committed prevents them; Repeatable Read prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents phantoms; Snapshot gives a consistent versioned view.
NOLOCK can also skip or double-read rows, not just read dirty data.
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) avoids readers blocking writers by reading row versions from tempdb.
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted allows all three; Repeatable Read stops non-repeatable reads; Serializable stops phantoms.
f: Why avoid NOLOCK?
It can return wrong results, including missing or duplicated rows.
Which isolation does RCSI give?
Read Committed using row versions, so readers don't block writers.

p5-34.a: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: rules and constraints hold. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives crashes, thanks to the transaction log.
p5-34.qa: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules and constraints hold after each transaction), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere beyond the isolation level) and Durability (committed data survives crashes, via the transaction log).
i: Write-ahead logging gives durability and rollback.
Distributed systems trade some ACID across services (sagas, eventual consistency).
Durability in SQL Server comes from write-ahead logging: the log record is hardened before commit returns.
Distributed services can't have ACID across databases cheaply, so we used outbox plus eventual consistency.
f: How does SQL Server guarantee durability?
Log records are hardened to disk before commit returns.
ACID vs BASE?
BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) describes many NoSQL systems.

p5-35.a: Optimistic: no locks; detect conflicts at write time with a rowversion; best for low contention (EF Core concurrency tokens).|Pessimistic: lock rows up front (UPDLOCK); for high-contention critical sections such as allocating the last drug kit.
p5-35.qa: Optimistic locking takes no locks; it detects conflicts at write time with a rowversion and fails the second writer, best for low contention (EF Core concurrency tokens). Pessimistic locking locks the row while working (SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK)), best for high contention like allocating the next randomization slot.
i: EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException; reload and retry or show a conflict.
APIs expose the version as an ETag with If-Match.
EF Core: a rowversion column marked IsRowVersion() gives optimistic concurrency; catch DbUpdateConcurrencyException and return 409.
c: public class Shipment { public int Id { get; set; } [Timestamp] public byte[] RowVersion { get; set; } = []; }
f: What does EF do with [Timestamp]?
Adds the version to the UPDATE WHERE clause and checks rows affected.
Risk of pessimistic locking?
Blocking and deadlocks if transactions are long.

p5-36.a: Measure first (Query Store, wait stats, slow queries), then fix the top queries (indexes, SARGable predicates, rewrites).|Schema: right data types and normalisation; keep statistics and index maintenance current.|Scale reads with caching and read replicas; archive or partition old data; short transactions and connection pooling.
p5-36.qa: Measure first (Query Store, wait stats, slow query logs), then fix the top queries (indexes, SARGable predicates, less data fetched, better joins), keep statistics fresh, shorten transactions, consider RCSI, cache hot reads, and scale hardware only after.
i: Wait stats tell where time goes (PAGEIOLATCH = I/O, LCK = blocking, CXPACKET = parallelism).
Batch and set-based operations instead of row by row.
Archive old data, partition very large tables.
Measure first: Query Store top resource consumers, wait stats, and actual execution plans before changing anything.
f: What do you check first?
Top queries by total CPU and duration in Query Store.
When would you partition?
Very large tables where sliding windows or maintenance per partition help.

p5-37.a: Start from real query patterns. Clustered key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing.|Non-clustered on foreign keys and filter columns, equality columns first then range, INCLUDE the selected columns.|Check usage DMVs, remove unused and duplicate indexes, and weigh the write cost.
p5-37.qa: Start from real query patterns. The clustered key should be narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing; add non-clustered indexes on foreign keys and frequent filters with equality columns first, INCLUDE columns to cover hot queries, filtered indexes for hot subsets, and remove unused or duplicate indexes. Verify with execution plans.
i: Avoid wide clustered keys: they're copied into every non-clustered index.
Consider write cost on busy tables.
Review missing index DMVs critically; they often over-suggest.
Design from queries: list the top queries' WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columns, then build the fewest indexes covering most of them.
f: Why ever-increasing clustered keys?
Inserts go to the end, reducing page splits and fragmentation.
Are missing index suggestions reliable?
They're hints; combine and validate them.

p5-38.a: An architecture of small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over APIs or messages.
p5-38.qa: Microservices are small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over APIs or messages. Teams can build, deploy and scale them separately.
i: Characteristics: database per service, decentralised governance, automated deployment, design for failure.
Size by business capability, not lines of code.
IRT services: randomization, supply, shipments, notifications.
Each service owns its data; sharing a database between services recreates a monolith.
f: Must each service have its own database?
Logically its own data, at least separate schemas with no cross-service access.
Microservices vs SOA?
Microservices are finer-grained, with smart endpoints and dumb pipes rather than an ESB.

p5-39.a: Advantages: independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy, technology choice per service.|Disadvantages: network latency and failures, distributed data and transactions, harder testing and debugging, more DevOps and observability work.
p5-39.qa: Advantages: independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy and technology choice per service. Disadvantages: distributed-system complexity (network failures, eventual consistency), harder testing and debugging, operational overhead (many pipelines, monitoring, tracing) and data consistency challenges.
i: Needs mature DevOps and observability.
Latency from network hops.
Advantages: independent deploys, scaling per service, fault isolation, team autonomy.
Disadvantages: network failures, distributed data consistency, more ops (observability, CI/CD per service).
f: Biggest hidden cost?
Operational complexity and data consistency across services.
How do you mitigate it?
Platform automation, templates, tracing and clear contracts.

p5-40.a: Small team or early product, unclear domain boundaries, low scale, no DevOps maturity (CI/CD, monitoring), or strong transactional consistency needed across the whole domain. Start with a modular monolith.
p5-40.qa: I wouldn't use microservices for a small team or early product, unclear domain boundaries, low scale, no DevOps maturity (CI/CD, monitoring), or when strong transactional consistency across the whole domain matters. A modular monolith is the better default.
i: Premature splitting creates a distributed monolith.
Extract services later along proven boundaries.
Small teams, unclear domains, or early products: start with a modular monolith and split on proven boundaries.
If services must always deploy together, they are a distributed monolith.
f: What is a modular monolith?
One deployable with strongly separated modules and boundaries.
Signal it's time to split?
Teams blocking each other or different scaling needs.

p5-41.a: Use Domain-Driven Design: split by business capability and bounded context, the area where one model and its language stay consistent (Randomization, Supply, Shipments, Consent).|Signals: separate data ownership, different change rates and teams, few chatty calls between them.
p5-41.qa: I use Domain-Driven Design: split by business capability and bounded context, the area where one model and its language are consistent (Randomization, Supply, Shipments). Signals include different data ownership, change frequency, team ownership and scaling needs; Event Storming workshops help find them.
i: A "Kit" means different things in Supply vs Dispensing: separate models.
Context maps describe relationships (customer-supplier, anti-corruption layer).
Avoid splitting by technical layer (a "data service").
Event storming with domain experts finds boundaries where language and data ownership change.
f: What is an anti-corruption layer?
A translation layer protecting your model from another system's model.
What is ubiquitous language?
Shared terms between developers and domain experts within a context.

p5-42.a: Synchronous REST or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer; asynchronous events or commands (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for decoupled workflows and notifications. Version every contract.
p5-42.qa: Synchronous REST or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer; asynchronous events or commands (Kafka, RabbitMQ) when it doesn't, to decouple services and absorb load. Prefer async for state changes others react to, and keep synchronous chains short.
i: gRPC for internal high-performance calls with contracts (Protobuf).
Events carry facts ("ShipmentDelivered"); commands request actions.
Always with timeouts, retries and idempotency.
Rule of thumb: sync for queries needing an immediate answer, async events for state changes others react to.
f: Why avoid long synchronous chains?
Latency adds up and one failure breaks the whole chain.
Events vs commands?
Events notify many about something that happened; commands tell one handler to do something.

p5-43.a: Synchronous (REST/gRPC): simple, immediate result, but temporal coupling; a slow callee slows the caller.|Asynchronous (queues/events): decoupled, absorbs spikes, resilient, but eventual consistency and harder tracing.
p5-43.qa: Synchronous (REST/gRPC) is simple with an immediate result but creates temporal coupling: a slow or down callee affects the caller. Asynchronous messaging decouples in time and absorbs spikes, enabling independent scaling, but adds eventual consistency, duplicate handling and harder debugging.
i: Request/reply over messaging exists but adds complexity.
Choose per interaction, not per system.
Sync chains multiply latency and failure probability: three services at 99.9% each give about 99.7% combined.
Async decouples availability but needs idempotency, ordering decisions and monitoring of lag.
f: Example of each in IRT?
REST to randomize a subject (needs an answer); Kafka events for shipment status changes.
How do you debug async flows?
Correlation ids, tracing and message logs.

p5-44.a: How services find each other's current addresses: DNS-based (Kubernetes Services, ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map) or load balancers, instead of hard-coded IPs as instances come and go.
p5-44.qa: Service discovery is how services find each other's current addresses: DNS-based (Kubernetes Services, ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map) or registry-based (Consul, Eureka), often behind load balancers. Clients call a stable name instead of IPs that change with scaling.
i: Client-side vs server-side discovery.
.NET Aspire provides service discovery for HttpClient (Microsoft.Extensions.ServiceDiscovery).
On ECS: Cloud Map or Service Connect; on Kubernetes: Services and DNS; behind an ALB, the ALB is the stable endpoint.
Client-side vs server-side discovery: client picks an instance from a registry vs a load balancer picks.
f: Why not hardcode IPs?
Containers come and go with changing IPs.
ECS Service Connect?
Managed service discovery and proxy for ECS services with metrics.

p5-45.a: Retrying non-idempotent operations duplicates side effects; retrying permanent errors (400, 401, validation) wastes effort; aggressive retries amplify load into retry storms.|Retry only transient errors, with backoff, jitter and limits.
p5-45.qa: Retrying non-idempotent operations duplicates side effects; retrying permanent errors (400, 401, validation) wastes resources; and retry storms from many clients amplify an outage. So I retry only transient errors (timeouts, 408, 429, 5xx), with exponential backoff and jitter, limited attempts, idempotency keys, and a circuit breaker.
i: Retry budgets limit total retries.
Respect Retry-After headers.
Retries at multiple layers multiply (3 × 3 × 3 = 27).
Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429 with Retry-After) and idempotent operations; use exponential backoff with jitter.
f: Why jitter?
To spread retries so clients don't retry in sync.
Example?
The Copilot retry suggestion that would have duplicated release creation (Part 3 Q35).

p5-46.a: Separate resource pools per dependency (connection pools, concurrency limits, queues) so one slow dependency cannot exhaust every thread or connection, like watertight compartments in a ship.
p5-46.qa: Bulkhead isolation uses separate resource pools per dependency (connection pools, concurrency limits, queues) so one slow dependency can't exhaust all threads or connections and take the whole service down. The name comes from ship compartments that contain flooding.
i: Polly concurrency limiter or ASP.NET Core rate limiting per dependency.
Separate HttpClients with their own handlers per downstream.
Separate worker pools or queues per workload type.
Polly v8 / Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience: the concurrency limiter strategy acts as a bulkhead.
f: Bulkhead vs circuit breaker?
Bulkhead limits resources used; circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency.
Example in IRT?
[Separate consumer pools for vendor file processing and notifications].

p5-47.a: Following one request across services with a trace id and spans (timing per hop), using OpenTelemetry and the W3C traceparent header; viewed in X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo to find where latency or errors happen.
p5-47.qa: Distributed tracing follows one request across services with a trace id and spans (timing per hop), using OpenTelemetry and W3C traceparent headers, visualised in X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo. It shows where latency and errors occur in a multi-service flow.
i: .NET has built-in Activity/ActivitySource; HttpClient and ASP.NET Core propagate context automatically.
Propagate through messages by putting traceparent in headers.
Sampling controls cost.
f: Trace id vs correlation id?
Similar purpose; trace ids are standardised and include parent-child spans.
How do you trace through RabbitMQ?
Inject traceparent into message headers and start a consumer span from it.

p5-48.a: Data across services becomes consistent after a short delay rather than instantly; accepted for availability and decoupling. Design UIs and processes to tolerate it, for example with Pending statuses.
p5-48.qa: Eventual consistency means data across services becomes consistent after a short delay rather than instantly, accepted for availability and decoupling. Design for it with idempotent consumers, clear UI states (Pending), versioning and reconciliation jobs.
i: Read-your-writes can be provided for the user who made the change.
Monitoring lag between services.
Users must see something sensible meanwhile, e.g. "Processing" status, not stale success.
Reconciliation jobs catch messages that went missing despite the outbox.
f: Where is it unacceptable in IRT?
Randomization slot allocation and kit assignment within a transaction.
How do you show it in a UI?
Status like "Processing" and refresh or push updates.

p5-49.a: Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks; asynchronous messaging with durable queues and DLQs; idempotency; sagas with compensations; monitoring and alerts.
p5-49.qa: Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks for synchronous calls; asynchronous messaging with durable queues and DLQs; idempotent handlers; sagas with compensation for multi-step workflows; and health checks with alerts.
i: Graceful degradation: show cached data when a dependency is down.
.NET 8 standard resilience handler bundles these for HttpClient.
Timeouts on every call, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks, and DLQs for async work.
Idempotent consumers so retries don't double-apply.
f: What is a fallback?
An alternative response when the call fails, like cached or default data.
What timeout values?
Based on the dependency's p99 plus margin, always less than the caller's own timeout.

p5-50.a: Version APIs (URL or header) and message contracts (additive changes, a schema version field); stay backward compatible; consumers tolerate unknown fields; deprecate with timelines; semantic-version the images.
p5-50.qa: Version APIs (URL segment or header) and message contracts (additive changes, a schema version field), stay backward compatible, use consumer-driven contract tests, and deprecate old versions with notice. Prefer additive, non-breaking changes so versions rarely change.
i: Tolerant reader: consumers ignore unknown fields.
Asp.Versioning library for ASP.NET Core.
Schema registry for Kafka (Avro/Protobuf compatibility rules).
Prefer backward-compatible changes (additive fields); version URLs (/v2) only for breaking changes, with a deprecation window.
f: What's a breaking change?
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings, new required inputs.
How long do you keep old versions?
Per agreement with consumers, with monitoring of usage.

p5-51.a: Each service has its own pipeline: build, test, image, IaC. Deploy independently to ECS or Kubernetes with rolling or blue-green strategies, health checks and automated rollback.
p5-51.qa: Each service has its own pipeline: build, test, image, IaC; deployments are independent to ECS or Kubernetes with rolling or blue-green strategies, health checks and automatic rollback, with configuration per environment and the same image promoted everywhere.
i: Shared pipeline templates for consistency.
Feature flags decouple release from deploy.
Contract tests prevent breaking consumers.
Each service has its own pipeline and artifact; rolling or blue/green deployments with health checks gate traffic.
f: How do you deploy a change spanning two services?
Make it backward compatible and deploy in order (provider first).
ECS deployment circuit breaker?
Stops and rolls back a deployment when tasks fail to become healthy.

p5-52.a: Golden signals per service, centralised structured logs with correlation ids, distributed tracing, Grafana or CloudWatch dashboards, and alerts on SLOs, queue lag and DLQ depth.
p5-52.qa: Golden signals per service, centralised structured logs with correlation ids, distributed tracing, Grafana or CloudWatch dashboards, SLOs with alerts, and business metrics such as shipments processed.
i: Same telemetry conventions across services (OpenTelemetry semantic conventions).
Dependency maps from traces.
Synthetic checks for critical flows.
Correlation ids across services (our [2024] middleware) let you follow one request through logs and traces.
f: What's an SLO?
A target like 99.9 percent of requests under 500 ms over 30 days.
Synthetic monitoring?
Scripted checks simulating user flows on a schedule (CloudWatch Synthetics).

p5-53.a: Private networking (VPC, security groups) plus mTLS where required; service identities (OAuth client-credentials tokens or IAM roles); validate tokens and scopes on every call; least privilege; secrets in a vault. Never trust a caller just because of its network location.
p5-53.qa: Private networking (VPC, security groups) plus mTLS where required; service identities (OAuth client credentials tokens or IAM roles) with authorization per call; secrets from a vault; and zero trust: never assume the internal network is safe.
i: Validate tokens audience-scoped per service.
Service mesh can provide mTLS automatically.
Least-privilege security group rules.
On AWS: IAM roles per task, security groups allowing only required ports, and TLS; JWT client-credentials for app-level identity.
f: Client credentials flow?
A service authenticates with its own credentials to get an access token for another API.
Why not trust internal traffic?
A compromised service could otherwise reach everything.

p5-54.a: Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, async queues to absorb spikes, caching and graceful degradation; avoid long synchronous call chains.
p5-54.qa: Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, async queues to absorb spikes, graceful degradation and fallbacks, and avoiding deep synchronous call chains.
i: Retry with backoff and budgets to avoid amplification.
Health checks shouldn't call dependencies deeply (avoid cascading restarts).
Timeouts shorter than the caller's, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding (429) and caches for read paths.
Avoid retry storms: retry budgets and jitter.
f: What is load shedding?
Rejecting excess requests early (503/429) to protect the system.
How do circuit breakers help?
They stop calls to a failing dependency, giving it time to recover and failing fast.

p5-55.a: Unit tests; integration tests with a real database and broker in containers; consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) between services; a few end-to-end tests; load and chaos tests for resilience.
p5-55.qa: Unit tests; integration tests with a real database and broker in containers (Testcontainers); consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) between services; a few end-to-end tests on critical flows; plus performance and resilience tests.
i: Test pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few E2E.
WebApplicationFactory for in-memory API tests.
.NET Aspire testing for distributed app tests.
Consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) catch breaking API changes before deploy.
f: Why contract tests?
They catch breaking API changes without full end-to-end environments.
Why not EF Core InMemory provider?
It behaves differently from real databases; use SQLite or Testcontainers.

p5-56.a: Environment variables plus central stores (AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, Azure App Configuration), per-environment values managed by IaC, no secrets in images, and validation at startup.
p5-56.qa: Environment variables plus central stores (AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, Azure App Configuration), per-environment values, validation at startup (ValidateOnStart), no secrets in code, and feature flags for runtime toggles.
i: Configuration providers layered in .NET: appsettings, environment, secrets, command line.
IOptionsMonitor for reload without restart.
Version and review config changes like code.
Parameter Store/Secrets Manager plus appsettings per environment; options validated on start.
f: How do you change config without redeploying?
Central store with reload (IOptionsMonitor) or feature flags.
Why validate at startup?
Missing config fails the deployment, not live requests (the UAT lesson).

p5-57.a: Structured JSON logs with correlation ids shipped to one place (CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, Loki), common fields (service, environment, version), retention policies, and no PHI or secrets.
p5-57.qa: Structured JSON logs with correlation ids shipped to one place (CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, Loki), common fields (service, environment, version, trace id), retention policies, no PHI or secrets, and queries and alerts on top.
i: Serilog or built-in JSON console logger.
Log levels set per category; avoid noisy debug in production.
Source-generated logging ([LoggerMessage]) for performance.
Structured JSON logs with correlation id, service name and environment fields make cross-service queries possible.
f: Why structured logs?
Fields can be queried and aggregated instead of parsing text.
How do you avoid logging PHI?
Redaction (Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance), reviewed log templates, and tests.

p5-58.a: API gateway in front of stateless services on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling.|Database per service, Redis caching, read replicas.|Async events via Kafka/RabbitMQ with outbox and idempotent consumers.|Observability, CI/CD per service and resilience patterns throughout.
p5-58.qa: An API gateway in front of stateless services on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling; database per service with Redis caching; async messaging for events; observability (logs, metrics, traces); CI/CD per service; resilience patterns; and multi-AZ deployment.
i: Start with clear bounded contexts.
Platform templates for new services.
Security: identity provider, mTLS or tokens between services.
Stateless services behind load balancers, autoscaling on CPU or queue depth, caching, and async processing for spikes.
f: What's the first bottleneck usually?
The database; plan indexing, caching and read replicas.
How do you handle cross-service queries?
API composition or read models built from events (CQRS).

p5-59.a: For synchronous request/response needs: UI and partner calls that need an immediate answer (get a study, randomize a subject), where the client must know the result now. REST is simple, cacheable and widely understood.
p5-59.qa: For synchronous request/response needs: UI and partner calls that need an immediate answer (get a study, randomize a subject). REST is simple, widely understood, works with gateways, caches and tools, and has standard semantics for status codes.
i: gRPC considered for internal high-throughput calls, but browser support and tooling favoured REST.
OpenAPI contracts for clients.
REST suits request/response queries from the React UI; HTTP caching and tooling (OpenAPI) are mature.
Messaging was used where the caller didn't need an immediate answer (shipment status updates).
f: Why not GraphQL?
Our clients have stable, known needs; GraphQL adds complexity for little gain.
When would you pick gRPC?
Internal, high-volume service-to-service calls with streaming.

p5-60.a: When producers should not wait for or know their consumers, several consumers need the same events, replay and retention matter, and throughput is high, for example shipment status events used by several services.
p5-60.qa: Kafka fits when producers shouldn't wait for or know their consumers, several consumers need the same events, replay and retention matter, and throughput is high, as with shipment status events consumed by several services.
i: Decoupling: new consumers added without changing producers.
Ordering per key (ShipmentId).
Replay for rebuilding read models or recovering.
Kafka keeps events for replay and multiple independent consumers; REST is point-to-point and immediate.
f: Downside?
Eventual consistency and operational complexity.
Why not RabbitMQ for that?
RabbitMQ deletes messages after consumption; Kafka keeps them for replay by multiple groups.

p5-61.a: Producers buffer and retry (idempotent producer, delivery timeout) and then fail, so write events to an outbox table and publish later; consumers pause and resume from committed offsets; alert on broker health.|A multi-broker cluster with replication avoids a single point of failure.
p5-61.qa: Producers buffer and retry (idempotent producer, delivery timeout) and then fail, so I write events to an outbox in the same transaction as the data and a relay publishes when Kafka is back; consumers resume from committed offsets; alerts fire on producer errors and consumer lag.
i: MSK multi-AZ with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 reduces outages.
acks=all for durability.
Producers buffer and retry (delivery.timeout.ms); after that, the app must persist to an outbox and resend.
Consumers simply pause and resume from committed offsets when the cluster returns.
f: What does acks=all mean?
The leader waits for all in-sync replicas before acknowledging.
How do you avoid losing events?
Outbox pattern plus idempotent consumers.

p5-62.a: True end-to-end exactly-once across systems is rarely possible; achieve effectively-once with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers (dedupe by message id, upserts) and the outbox pattern.|Inside Kafka, idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once read-process-write.
p5-62.qa: True end-to-end exactly-once across systems is rarely possible; I achieve effectively-once with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers (inbox table or upserts), the outbox pattern on the producer side, and Kafka transactions for read-process-write within Kafka.
i: Store offsets with data in the same transaction for Kafka-to-DB.
Deduplicate by message id with a unique constraint.
Kafka transactions plus idempotent producers give exactly-once within Kafka (read-process-write).
With external side effects (database, email), use at-least-once plus idempotent consumers (processed-message table).
f: What is Kafka EOS?
Exactly-once semantics using idempotent producers and transactions within Kafka.
Why isn't it end-to-end?
External side effects (DB writes, emails) aren't part of Kafka's transaction.

p5-63.a: Requests come through API Gateway or an ALB to .NET Core services in Docker on ECS, in private subnets across two availability zones.|Data in RDS SQL Server (Multi-AZ) and DynamoDB, ElastiCache for caching, Lambda for event-driven pieces.|Logs and metrics in CloudWatch, dashboards in Grafana; infrastructure in CloudFormation and Terraform, deployed through Azure DevOps.
p5-63.qa: Requests come through API Gateway or an ALB to .NET services in Docker on ECS, in private subnets across availability zones; data lives in RDS SQL Server and DynamoDB, with ElastiCache for caching; events go through Kafka (MSK) and RabbitMQ; Lambda handles event-driven tasks; S3 stores files; secrets come from Secrets Manager; CloudWatch and Grafana monitor; and IaC plus Azure DevOps pipelines deploy it.
i: Draw layers: edge (Route 53, WAF, ALB/API Gateway), compute (ECS Fargate), data, messaging, observability.
Security: task roles, security groups, VPC endpoints, KMS encryption.
HA: multi-AZ for ALB, ECS, RDS and MSK.
Only describe what you can defend; say which parts you worked on most.
f: Why both RDS and DynamoDB?
Relational data with transactions in RDS; high-scale key-value access patterns (idempotency, sessions) in DynamoDB.
How do vendors connect?
SFTP integrations and APIs through the gateway.

p5-64.a: It was the company's chosen cloud for IRT. Its managed services (ECS, RDS, Lambda, DynamoDB) reduce operations work, it supports compliance for regulated workloads, and it has global regions and mature IaC tooling.
p5-64.qa: AWS was the company's chosen cloud for IRT; its managed services (ECS, RDS, Lambda, DynamoDB) reduce operational work, it has strong compliance programmes for life sciences, global regions for data residency, and mature IaC and security tooling.
i: Managed services let small teams focus on features.
Compliance: HIPAA eligibility, GxP guidance from AWS.
Honest answer: it was an organisational decision; I can explain the benefits.
Company standard plus managed services (RDS, ECS Fargate, ElastiCache) reduce ops for a small team.
f: Would you pick Azure instead?
Either works; choose by company skills, existing contracts and services.
What's the biggest AWS benefit for you?
Managed infrastructure with fine-grained IAM.

p5-65.a: ECS: AWS-native, simpler, deep IAM and ALB integration, no control-plane fee.|EKS: managed Kubernetes, portable, huge ecosystem, but more complexity and cost.|Choose ECS for AWS-only simplicity, EKS to standardise on Kubernetes.
p5-65.qa: ECS is AWS-native, simpler, with deep IAM and ALB integration and no control-plane fee; EKS is managed Kubernetes, portable across clouds with a large ecosystem, but more complex and with a control-plane fee. Both can run on Fargate or EC2.
i: ECS fits AWS-only teams wanting less operational load.
EKS fits Kubernetes skills, multi-cloud, or ecosystem needs (Helm, operators, service mesh).
EKS Auto Mode (2024) reduces node management.
ECS is simpler and AWS-native; EKS gives Kubernetes portability and ecosystem at higher operational cost.
f: Which does IRT use?
ECS for production services.
Can you move from ECS to EKS later?
Yes; containers are portable, but deployment definitions change.

p5-66.a: Serverless compute for containers on ECS or EKS: you set CPU and memory per task and AWS runs it, with no EC2 instances to patch or scale.
p5-66.qa: Fargate is serverless compute for containers on ECS or EKS: you set CPU and memory per task and AWS runs it, with no EC2 instances to patch, scale or secure. You pay per vCPU and GB per second.
i: Each task gets its own isolated kernel boundary and ENI.
Fargate Spot for interruptible workloads at a discount.
Limits: no privileged containers or daemon sets; ephemeral storage up to 200 GB.
You pay per vCPU and memory per second; no EC2 patching, but less control (no daemonsets, GPU limited).
f: Fargate vs EC2 launch type cost?
Fargate costs more per unit but saves operations; EC2 is cheaper at steady high utilisation.
Can you SSH into Fargate?
Use ECS Exec for a shell instead.

p5-67.a: API Gateway: API management features: auth (JWT, Lambda authorizers), throttling, usage plans, request validation, direct Lambda integration; priced per request.|ALB: layer 7 load balancing for HTTP to ECS/EC2 targets, path and host routing, cheaper at high steady volume, fewer API features.
p5-67.qa: API Gateway provides API management: auth (JWT, Lambda authorizers), throttling, usage plans, request validation, transformations and direct Lambda integration, priced per request. ALB is a layer 7 load balancer for containers and instances: cheaper at high steady traffic, path and host routing, WebSockets and long connections, priced per hour and LCU.
i: Use both: API Gateway for external APIs, ALB for internal services.
API Gateway has a default 29-second integration timeout; ALB idle timeout is configurable up to 4000 seconds.
API Gateway: auth, throttling, usage plans, request validation; ALB: cheaper at high request volume, path/host routing to containers.
HTTP API (API Gateway v2) is cheaper and faster than REST API when advanced features aren't needed.
f: Which for high-volume internal traffic?
ALB, for cost and simplicity.
Can ALB authenticate users?
Yes, with OIDC or Cognito authentication actions.

p5-68.a: Serverless functions that run on events (API Gateway, S3, SQS, DynamoDB Streams, schedules); you pay per request and duration; scaling is automatic; maximum 15 minutes per run.
p5-68.qa: Lambda runs functions on events (API Gateway, S3, SQS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge schedules); you pay per request and duration, and AWS manages servers and scaling. It supports managed .NET LTS runtimes (.NET 8 and newer as AWS adds them), plus custom runtimes or container images, up to 15 minutes per invocation and 10 GB memory.
i: Event source mappings poll SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams.
Cold starts; mitigate with SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, AOT.
Lambda Powertools for .NET for logging, metrics, tracing and idempotency.
Cold starts for .NET can be reduced with Native AOT or SnapStart (supported for .NET managed runtimes since late 2024).
f: Is Lambda good for APIs?
For spiky or low traffic, yes; for steady high traffic, containers are often cheaper.
What runs your Lambda .NET code?
The managed .NET runtime or a container image with the Lambda runtime interface.

p5-69.a: The number of executions running at the same time. Accounts have a regional limit (1,000 by default); reserved concurrency caps or guarantees a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm; excess requests are throttled.
p5-69.qa: Lambda concurrency is the number of executions running at the same time. Accounts have a regional limit (1,000 by default, raisable); reserved concurrency guarantees and caps a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialised to avoid cold starts.
i: Throttling returns 429 for sync calls; async events retry.
Reserved concurrency of 0 disables a function (an emergency stop).
Protect downstream databases by capping concurrency.
Reserved concurrency caps a function to protect downstream databases; provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm.
f: How do you protect RDS from Lambda scaling?
Reserved concurrency plus RDS Proxy for connection pooling.
Reserved vs provisioned?
Reserved limits and guarantees capacity; provisioned pre-warms environments for latency.

p5-70.a: The maximum run time per invocation, configurable up to 15 minutes. Set it a little above the expected duration, align it with upstream timeouts (API Gateway has a 29-second default), and move longer work to Step Functions or ECS.
p5-70.qa: The timeout is the maximum run time per invocation, configurable up to 15 minutes. Set it a little above the expected duration, set downstream timeouts below it, and move long work to queues, Step Functions or ECS.
i: SQS visibility timeout should be at least 6x the function timeout (AWS guidance).
API Gateway caps synchronous calls at its integration timeout.
Monitor Duration p99 against the timeout.
Max timeout is 15 minutes; API Gateway has its own integration timeout (29 s by default) that can cut off earlier.
f: What happens on timeout?
The invocation is stopped; async events retry; stream batches retry.
Why set downstream timeouts lower?
So the function can handle failures cleanly instead of being killed.

p5-71.a: A fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, on-demand or provisioned capacity, streams, TTL and global tables.
p5-71.qa: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, on-demand or provisioned capacity, global tables, streams, TTL and transactions. You design tables around access patterns.
i: Partition key plus optional sort key; GSIs and LSIs for other access patterns.
Strongly consistent reads optional (not on GSIs).
On-demand pricing cut significantly in late 2024, making it the default choice for many.
Design access patterns first; partition key choice determines scalability (avoid hot partitions).
f: When not to use DynamoDB?
Ad-hoc queries, complex joins and reporting; use relational or analytics stores.
Does it support transactions?
Yes, TransactWriteItems across up to 100 items.

p5-72.a: GSI (global secondary index): a different partition and sort key, its own capacity, created any time, eventually consistent reads.|LSI (local secondary index): same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, supports strongly consistent reads, 10 GB per partition-key limit.
p5-72.qa: A GSI (global secondary index) has a different partition and sort key, its own capacity, can be created any time and is eventually consistent; an LSI (local secondary index) keeps the same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, supports strong consistency and limits each partition key's item collection to 10 GB.
i: Project only needed attributes to save cost.
Sparse indexes: only items with the attribute appear.
GSI throttling can back-pressure writes to the base table.
GSIs are eventually consistent and can be added anytime; LSIs must be created with the table and share its partition key.
f: When use an LSI?
Rarely; when you need strongly consistent alternate sort orders within a partition.
What is a sparse index?
A GSI on an attribute that only some items have, giving a cheap filtered view.

p5-73.a: RDS: a managed relational database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others) with automated backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and read replicas.|EC2-hosted: full control of the OS and settings, but you own patching, backups and high availability. Choose RDS unless you need that control.
p5-73.qa: RDS is a managed relational database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, plus Aurora) with automated backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas and monitoring. An EC2-hosted database gives full control (OS, unsupported features, custom agents) but you own backups, HA, patching and scaling.
i: RDS Custom for SQL Server when you need OS-level access.
Point-in-time restore from automated backups.
Performance Insights for query analysis.
RDS handles backups, patching and Multi-AZ failover; EC2 gives OS control at the cost of running it yourself.
f: When choose EC2?
Features RDS doesn't support or special licensing needs.
What does Multi-AZ do?
Maintains a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.

p5-74.a: Redis: in memory, sub-millisecond reads, rich data structures and TTL; ideal for caches, sessions, rate limits and locks, but not the system of record.|Database: durable, queryable, transactional source of truth.
p5-74.qa: Redis is in-memory with sub-millisecond reads, rich data structures and TTLs, ideal for caches, sessions, rate limits, locks and leaderboards; a database is the durable system of record with queries, transactions and constraints. Redis complements a database rather than replacing it.
i: Redis persistence (RDB/AOF) exists but isn't a substitute for a primary DB in most designs.
Valkey is the open-source fork after Redis licence changes in 2024; ElastiCache supports it.
Cache invalidation and consistency need design.
Our logout denylist used ElastiCache Redis keyed by jti with TTL equal to token expiry: [~1 ms] lookups.
f: Can Redis lose data?
Yes, on failover or eviction, so cache data must be rebuildable.
Why Valkey?
An open-source, Linux Foundation fork, cheaper on ElastiCache.

p5-75.a: Block Public Access, least-privilege bucket policies and IAM, encryption at rest (SSE-KMS) and in transit (HTTPS-only policy), versioning and Object Lock where needed, presigned URLs for temporary access, access logs and CloudTrail, VPC endpoints.
p5-75.qa: Block Public Access, least-privilege bucket policies and IAM, encryption at rest (SSE-KMS) and in transit (HTTPS-only policy with aws:SecureTransport), versioning and Object Lock where needed, short-lived presigned URLs, access logging or CloudTrail data events, and VPC endpoint policies.
i: Disable ACLs (Object Ownership: bucket owner enforced, default since 2023).
New objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default since 2023.
Macie to find sensitive data.
f: SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS?
KMS adds key policies, audit and rotation control.
What is Object Lock?
WORM retention that prevents deletion or overwrite for a period.

p5-76.a: IAM controls who can do what on which AWS resources, through users, groups, roles and policies.|User: a long-term identity with credentials, for people (prefer SSO).|Role: an assumable identity with temporary credentials, for services (ECS task role, Lambda) and cross-account access; preferred.
p5-76.qa: IAM controls who can do what on which AWS resources through users, groups, roles and policies. A user is a long-term identity with credentials (password, access keys); a role is assumed temporarily by services, apps or people and gives short-lived credentials, the preferred approach.
i: Workloads use roles (ECS task role, Lambda execution role, EC2 instance profile).
People use IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of IAM users.
STS AssumeRole for cross-account access.
Prefer roles with temporary credentials everywhere; users with long-lived keys are a common breach source.
f: Why avoid access keys?
They're long-lived and leak easily; roles rotate credentials automatically.
What is a trust policy?
The part of a role defining who can assume it.

p5-77.a: Logs: detailed event records, searchable with Logs Insights.|Metrics: numeric time series (CPU, latency, errors) for graphs and alarms; metric filters can turn log patterns into metrics.
p5-77.qa: CloudWatch Logs holds detailed event records, searchable with Logs Insights; CloudWatch Metrics are numeric time series (CPU, latency, errors) for graphs and alarms. Logs explain what happened; metrics show trends and trigger alerts cheaply.
i: Metric filters derive metrics from logs.
Embedded Metric Format: emit metrics inside structured logs.
Logs cost per GB ingested; metrics per metric and API call.
Metric filters can turn log patterns into metrics, which alarms can then watch.
f: How long are metrics kept?
Up to 15 months with decreasing resolution.
How do you search logs across services?
Logs Insights queries across multiple log groups.

p5-78.a: Rules that watch a metric against a threshold over periods (for example 5xx over 1 percent for 5 minutes) and change state between OK and ALARM, triggering SNS notifications, autoscaling or other actions; composite alarms reduce noise.
p5-78.qa: CloudWatch alarms watch a metric against a threshold over periods (e.g. 5xx over 1 percent for 5 minutes) and move between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, triggering actions like SNS notifications, autoscaling or EC2 actions.
i: Composite alarms combine conditions to reduce noise.
Anomaly detection bands for seasonal metrics.
"M out of N" datapoints to avoid flapping.
Treat missing data deliberately (notBreaching, breaching).
f: How do you avoid alert noise?
Composite alarms, sensible periods and alerting on symptoms.
Missing data setting for a heartbeat metric?
Treat as breaching so silence triggers the alarm.

p5-79.a: Check scope and recent changes; CloudWatch dashboards and alarms (ALB 5xx, target health, ECS task restarts, RDS CPU and connections); Logs Insights by correlation id; ECS events (OOM kills, failed health checks); CloudTrail for config changes; AWS Health for service issues. Mitigate, then fix the cause.
